full_judgment:
13. Prosecution, in proof of culpability of Mahbubuddin and Belal, placed on witness box sixteen (16) witnesses. Out of sixteen (16) witnesses PW s. 1-7 and 10 were nearest and closest relations of deceased Nilufar through blood. PW 1 HR Khan was the father of deceased Nilufar. He drafted and processed first information report dated 2-12-1992 which Mahbubuddin carried to Sabujbagh Police Station. He was the author of Petition of Complaint dated 4-6-1994 before Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka and Petition of Complaint had been registered as Sabujbagh Police Station Case No.69(6)94 on being treated as First Information Report. He drew his last breath during course of cross-examination without drawing an end to cross examination. He could not be cross-examined fully and his cross-examination remained incomplete. PW 2 Anjumanara Rashid was the .mother of deceased Nilufar. PW 3 Khairunnessa alias Rinu was the sister of PW 2. PW 4 Rowshanara Mahmud was the sister's daughter of PW 2. PW 5 Lutfunnessa was sister of PW 2. PW 6 Suriya Chowdhury was the sister of deceased Nilufar and daughter of PW 1 and PW 2. PW 7 Dr Abdul Rashid was the son of PW 3. PW 8 SM Shahadat Hossain was a Doctor. PW 9 Younus Chowdhury was a neighbour to crime house PW 10 Jalalur and 2. PW 11 Azharul Islam, Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka at the time of occurrence recorded Judicial confessional statement of Md Belal and he proved Judicial confessional statement which was exhibited as Exhibit 3. PW 12 Dr Pronab Kumar Chakravorty performed Post Mortem Examination on the dead body of Nilufar and laid Report and he offered evidence in support of Post Mortem Report which is exhibited as Exhibit 4. PW 13 Md Abdus Sabur performed Inquest on dead body of Nilufar and substituted Inquest report which was exhibited as Exhibit-5. He proved first information report dated 2-12-1992. He performed partial investigation of Sabujbagh Police Station Case No. 4(12)92 PW 14 Munshi Atiqur Rahman. Police Personnel, also, carried on investigation of Sabujbagh Police Station Case No. 4(l2)92 and, thereafter, handed over case diary to Additional Superintendent of Police Mr Kahar Akhand (PW 16). PW 15 Md Shafiuzzaman, Assistant Commissioner of Detective Branch or Dhaka Metropolitan Police, also, carried on investigation as Investigating Officer of Sabujbagh Police Station Case No.4(12)92 and, also, of Sabujbagh Police Station Case No.69(6)94. PW 16 Md Abdul Kahar Akhand was the last and final Investigating Officer of the case and he submitted Police Report in the form of charge-sheet against Mahbubuddin and Md Belal. 

 I. Deceased Nilufar had been killed in the house of convict appellant and convict-appellant was required to account for the cause of death of his wife Nilufar and convict-appellant failed to discharge the special onus upon him in proof of his innocence Plea of "alibi" adopted from side of convict- appellant on production of defence witnesses could not be proved and plea of "alibi" fell to ground and Trial Judge was well justified in awarding conviction and sentence upon convict-appellant on finding him guilty of charge levelled against him and no interference is called for by this Court in the exercise of its appellate authority. Evidence of PW 9 Younus Chowdhury had been referred to in support of contention. 

 24. Fundamental and basic principles in the Administration of Criminal Law and Justice Delivery System is the innocence of alleged accused and till charges are proved beyond shadow of doubt on the basis of clear, cogent, credible and unimpeachable evidence, question of indicting or punishing an accused' does not arise. Justice delivery system cannot be carried away by heinous nature of crime or by gruesome manner in which it was found to have been committed. Mere suspicion, however strong or probable it might be, is no effective substitute for legal proof required to substantiate the charge of commission of crime and graver the charge is greater is the standard of proof required. Courts dealing with criminal eases at least constantly remember that there is a long mental distance between "may be true" and "must be true" and this Basic and Golden Rule only helps to maintain the vital distinction between "conjecture" and "sure conclusions" to be reached on the touchstone of dispassionate Judicial scrutiny based upon a complete and comprehensive appreciation of features of the case as well as quality and credibility of evidence brought on record. In appreciating the evidence of a prosecution witness the approach must be whether the evidence of a witness carries a ring of truth or evidence is tainted with falsehood and Court got an arduous duty to scrutinise the evidence more carefully keeping in view the deficiency, drawback, infirmity, discrepancy coming out from the mouth of prosecution witnesses and to separate truth from falsehood and grain from chaff. 

 26. On legal burden of proving guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the oft-quoted observation of Lord Sankey LC in Woolmington vs Director of Public Prosecutions (1935) AC 462 may be noticed which are couched in following language: 

 74. A case was, also, faintly strived to be built up by prosecution from the mouth of PW 2 that convict-appellant on a query from his" son Pasha disclosed that he "was the author of biting on shoulder of Nilufar. But the case was not at all ventured to be proved by prosecution in calling PW 2's son Pasha as witness on witness box. Futile labour undertaken by prosecution could not be carried to a successful point. Testimonies offered by PW 10 that he believed the marks of biting to be of Mahbub (convict-appellant) is, also, of no avail to prosecution inasmuch as belief is only belief and belief is no substitute of proof. 

 83. It came into view from testimony of PW 16, the last and final Investigating Officer who laid charge-sheet that in the charge-sheet name of 27 persons had been noted and Nur Mohammad, driver of car of Mahbub (convict-appellant), Ismail, caretaker of crime building, Ms Ratna, a tenant of incident building and Halirna Chowdhury, another tenant of occurrence building had been cited as witness Nos. 20, 21,19 and 25 respectively. PW 13, one of the Investigating Officers, in his evidence disclosed that he recorded statement of Ismail under section 161 of The Code. It also, came out from the account of PW 15, one of the Investigating Officers, that he recorded the statement of Ismail under section 161 of the Code on 19-8-1994. Ismail was a very material witness and though his statement was recorded by two Investigating Officers PW 13 and PW 15 he was not examined as a witness by prosecution during trial. It emerged from the testimony of PW 16 that he recorded the statement of Azaharul Islam (DW 6) under section 161 of The Code and made him a charge-sheet witness. AzaharuI Islam had not been, also, examined by prosecution rather he had been examined as DW 6 in proof of defence case of alibi programmed by convict-appellant. It had been further blurted out from evidence of PW 16 that none of the neighbouring people of crime building were witnesses in the case. Name of Nur Mohammad, driver of the car of Mahbub (convict-appellant) came into picture from mouth of PW 1 himself in his declaration before trial Court that on 2-12-1992 at about 2-00 PM (noon) Nur Mohammad came to his house and supplied him information that his daughter Nilu (Nilufar) had been murdered. This Nur Mohammad could be an important and material witness in unveiling the murder episode of deceased Nilufar Ismail, care-taker of crime building, Ms Ratna and Halima Chowdhury, tenants of occurrence building who were cited as witnesses in charge-sheet and neighboring people of crime building had not been produced on witness box in proof of prosecution case in regard to embroilment of convict-appellant in the crime. Withholding of the above material witnesses in the background of fact and circumstances of the case was fatal to the structure of prosecution case and an adverse inference against prosecution case for non- examination of above witnesses legitimately might arise and virtually arose. The inevitable legal presumption springing out of non-examination of the above witnesses/persons is that if those witnesses/persons would have been examined they would not have definitely supported the prosecution case in bridgement of convict-appellant in the murder of his wife Nilufar. On this score, also, convict-appellant is entitled to get the benefit of doubt. 

 86. Contention pressed into. service from side of State-respondent that deceased Nilufar was found dead in house of convict-appellant and convict- appellant was to account for cause of death of Nilufar and special onus lay on him to lay proof that he was not the killer of Nilufar is now given attention to. 

 98. Plea adopted by convict-appellant was a plea of "alibi". The word "alibi" is of Latin origin and means "elsewhere". "Alibi" is a Rule of Evidence and it flows from section 11 of The Evidence Act. It is a convenient term used for the defence taken by an accused that when the occurrence took place he was so far away from the place of occurrence that it is highly improbable that he would have participated in the crime. The theory of "alibi", according to Wig more on Evidence, is that the fact of presence elsewhere is essentially inconsistent with the presence at the place and time alleged, and therefore with personal participation in the act. The defence of alibi is a legitimate defence and, in fact, is often the only evidence of an innocent person. "It is really positive evidence which in the nature of things necessarily implies a negative" (Foster, Discussion on the Crown Law). The burden of proving commission of offence by the accused so as to fasten the liability of guilt on him remains on the prosecution and would not be lessened by the mere fact that the accused had adopted the defence of alibi. The plea of alibi taken by the accused needs to be considered only when the burden which lies on the prosecution has been discharged satisfactorily. If the prosecution has failed in discharging its burden of proving the commission of crime by the accused beyond any reasonable doubt, it may not be necessary to go into the question whether the accused has succeeded in proving the defence of alibi. But once the prosecution succeeds in discharging its burden then it is incumbent on the accused taking the plea of alibi to prove it with certainty so as to exclude the possibility of his presence at the place and time of occurrence. An obligation is cast on the Court to weigh in scales the evidence adduced by the prosecution in proving the guilt of the accused and the evidence adduced by the accused in proving his defence of alibi. If the evidence adduced by the accused is of such a quality and of such a standard that the Court may entertain some reasonable doubt regarding his presence at the place and time of occurrence, the Court would evaluate the prosecution evidence to see if the evidence adduced on behalf of the prosecution leaves any slot available to fit therein the defence of alibi. While weighing the prosecution case and the defence case, pitted against each other, if the balance tilts in favour of the accused, the prosecution would fail and the accused would be entitled to the benefit of that reasonable doubt which would emerge in the mind of the Court. 

 ''It is to be remembered that if the plea of alibi is not believed, it does not necessarily follow that the prisoner committed the murder. The prosecution is to prove the guilt of the accused and failure on the part of the defence to substantiate any plea taken by it does not necessarily prove the guilt of the accused. According to the settled principle of law, the burden to prove the guilt of the accused is primarily and principally upon the prosecution. 

 104. The word "abscondence" is derived from Latin term "abscondore" which means "to hide". Law on abscondence is well settled. Abscondence of an accused does not automatically amount to offence of guilty mind and abscondence is equally consistent with innocence and guilt. Abscondence cannot always be an incriminating circumstances to lead to inference of guilt of accused person. Of course, abscondence of accused in the fact and circumstances of a case, sometimes, may furnish corroboration of prosecution evidence but it is established principle of Administration of Criminal Justice that mere abscondence is no proof of guilt of an accused. Munir in his Law of Evidence (1974 Edition) observes' at page 61: 

 "(1) The facts alleged as the basis of any legal inference must be clearly proved and beyond reasonable doubt connected with the factum probandum; (2) the burden of proof is always on the party who asserts the existence of any fact, which infers legal accountability; (3) in all cases, whether of direct or circumstantial evidence, the best evidence must be adduced which the nature of the case admits; (4) in order to justify the inference of guilt, the inculpatory facts must be incompatible with the innocence of the accused and incapable of explanation, upon any other reasonable hypothesis than that of his guilt; and (5) if there be any reasonable doubt of the guilt of the accused, he is entitled as of right to be acquitted". 

 128. Circumstances relied upon by prosecution do not at all form rosary and they are mere beads. Chain is completely snuffed. Circumstances relied upon by prosecution do not unerringly point guilt towards convict-appellant and those are not consistent with his guilt. Circumstances do not at all warrant a conclusion of murder by convict-appellant. Learned Trial Judge did not endeavor to find out whether each and every incriminating circumstances in bridging convict-appellant in the offence had been clearly established by reliable and clinching evidence. Innocence of convict-appellant cannot be excluded altogether, and if innocence of accused cannot be excluded altogether, convict-appellant cannot be the victim of suspicion. Suspicion, however, strong cannot take the place of proof. 

 133. In the case in hand evidence and materials relied upon by prosecution to fasten guilt upon convict-appellant only points needle of suspicion towards convict-appellant and nothing more. Suspicion, however, strong is no substitute for proof and in Criminal Law the prosecution is to prove the guilt of accused beyond reasonable doubt. Offence alleged in the present case being murder which visits the perpetrator of crime with the minimum sentence of imprisonment for life, a Court of law is to be justified in demanding full satisfaction before lethality of section 302 of Penal Code can be pressed into service against convict-appellant. The evidence and materials on record and fact and circumstances of the case are not such as to penetrate the fortress of innocence built around convict-appellant. The evidence, materials on record, fact and circumstances of the case fall below the standard required to be achieved by prosecution to demand conviction and sentence upon convict-appellant.
